messages.content: The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I'm spending about ten hours a week maintaining a tool I built. Is that worth it?

Compare it against what those ten hours would otherwise produce, not against zero. If a commercial equivalent costs less than the value of that time, the tool is costing you more than it saves regardless of how well it works. The sunk build effort shouldn't enter the calculation.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our team spends two days a month on a report nobody seems to read.

Test it: skip an issue and see who asks. Twenty-four days a year is a substantial recurring cost against an unmeasured benefit, and the experiment costs one cycle. If nobody notices, you've found free capacity.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We could build this integration ourselves or pay a vendor. How do I decide?

Price the build at engineering time plus perpetual maintenance, which is the part that gets omitted and usually dominates. Then ask whether the integration is something you'd want to differentiate on. Building what you compete on is worth a premium; building commodity plumbing rarely is.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Two candidates: one is clearly stronger but wants 30% more.

Estimate the output difference rather than the credential difference. If the stronger candidate genuinely produces more than 30% more value in the role, the premium is underpriced. Where roles have a ceiling on individual output — a lot of them do — the cheaper candidate wins on arithmetic.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I've been offered overtime at time-and-a-half. Worth it?

Depends what the hours displace. If they come out of recovery, the premium is buying hours that reduce the quality of the hours you're already paid for, and the true rate is lower than it looks. If they come out of genuinely idle time, it's straightforwardly good.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How much research should I do before making a decision?

Until additional research stops changing your leading option. That's the practical stopping rule, and it's usually reached much earlier than comfort suggests. Research past that point is buying confidence rather than information.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it worth optimizing a process that runs twice a year?

Almost never, unless the failure cost is high or the knowledge decays between runs. Multiply the saving by two and compare against the optimization effort — for most twice-yearly processes the arithmetic is unfavourable and the real win is documentation, not automation.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I keep getting asked to do small favours that each take twenty minutes.

Count the frequency. Twenty minutes twice a week is thirty hours a year, which is a meaningful project's worth of time being spent invisibly because no individual instance is large enough to notice. That's the number to evaluate against, not the twenty minutes.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I compare a certain small gain against a possible large one?

Compute the expected value, then check whether you can survive the bad branch and whether you get to repeat the bet. Expected value is the right guide across many independent decisions and a poor guide for a single decision with an outcome you can't absorb.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I weigh employee satisfaction against short-term output?

Price the turnover. Replacing someone costs several months of productivity plus recruitment, so a satisfaction problem that raises attrition is an output problem on a delay. The two only look opposed when the horizon is short enough to exclude the consequences.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're assuming 20% growth. How do I sanity-check that?

Decompose it. Growth is some combination of new customers, expansion, and retention — check whether each component's implied number is something you've achieved before. Aggregate targets survive scrutiny that their components don't.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we spend on a marketing push now or reinvest in the product?

Ask what happens to acquired users at the current product quality. Marketing into a product with poor retention buys a leaky bucket, and the spend is recoverable only if they stay. If retention is solid, marketing compounds; if it isn't, the product spend has to come first.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I'm choosing between two suppliers, one cheaper and one more reliable.

Price the unreliability. Estimate how often the cheaper one fails, what a failure costs you in delay and rework, and add that to their quote. Reliability premiums are frequently correct once the failure cost is actually computed rather than assumed to be small.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I evaluate a long-term investment when I can't predict the market?

Shift the question from prediction to robustness: which option is least bad across the range of futures you consider plausible? Optimizing for the expected case produces something fragile, and the expected case is the one thing you can be fairly confident won't happen exactly.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We want to move upmarket to larger customers.

Predict the changes that follow: longer sales cycles, procurement, security review, feature demands that don't help smaller customers, and support expectations that change your cost structure. The revenue per customer rises and so does the cost to serve, often faster than expected.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our churn is 5% monthly and we're focused on acquisition.

That's roughly half your customer base annually, so acquisition is refilling rather than growing. Retention improvements compound against every future cohort while acquisition spend applies once. Unless the acquisition cost is unusually low, the retention work has the better return.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I evaluate an option nobody has tried?

Estimate the range rather than a point, and identify the cheapest test that would move the range. Novel options are usually evaluated against an unfairly precise picture of the familiar one, which biases toward the status quo.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I keep polishing presentations well past the point of usefulness.

Estimate what an extra hour changes in the audience's decision. For most internal presentations the answer is nothing after the content is clear and the numbers are right. Set a time budget proportional to what the presentation is actually deciding.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I value something that only pays off if several things go right?

Multiply the probabilities and look at the result honestly. Chains of individually likely steps produce surprisingly low joint probabilities, and plans with four 80% dependencies succeed about 40% of the time. That number is usually much lower than the plan's authors expect.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We've spent six months on a feature with no clear finish line.

Define what shipping requires today and cut to that. Six months without a finish line usually means the definition of done keeps moving, and the marginal work is being chosen by whoever is closest to it rather than by value. Set the criterion externally.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We've invested two years in a platform that isn't working out.

The two years are spent regardless of what you choose now, so exclude them. Ask what you'd pick if you were starting today with current knowledge. If the answer is a different platform, the only question left is migration cost against continued drag.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I've nearly finished a certification I've realized I don't need.

Compare the remaining cost against the remaining benefit. 'Nearly finished' is doing persuasive work it hasn't earned — if there's genuinely little left and some residual value, finish it; if there's substantial effort left and no use for it, stopping is correct however uncomfortable.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our contract has six months left and the service is poor.

Compare the cost of switching now against six months of degraded service plus the switching cost later, which you'll pay either way. Contracts feel binding in a way that makes people absorb more than the arithmetic justifies.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I decide when I don't have enough information?

Ask whether the decision is reversible. Reversible decisions should be made quickly on partial information and treated as experiments; irreversible ones justify the delay of gathering more. Applying the same care to both is the common and expensive mistake.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we hire a permanent employee or a contractor?

Depends on the certainty of the need. Contractors cost more per hour and less to unwind, so they're the right choice while demand is uncertain. Once the need is proven and ongoing, permanent hiring is cheaper and retains knowledge that otherwise leaves.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I structure a deal with someone I can't fully assess?

Reduce exposure rather than trying to reduce uncertainty. A smaller first commitment, staged milestones, and an exit that doesn't need their cooperation all substitute for information you can't obtain.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're choosing between reducing costs and improving quality.

Find out whether quality is currently costing you revenue. If defects are driving churn or support load, quality improvement is a cost reduction with a longer lag, and the two aren't opposed. If quality is already above what customers notice, further investment there has poor returns.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we prioritize the feature many users want a little or the one few users need badly?

Ask which one changes behaviour. Mild broad preference frequently produces no measurable change in retention or usage, while an acute need for a small segment can anchor them permanently. Intensity often beats breadth, particularly early.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I forecast the impact of a change we've never made before?

Find the closest analogue, internal or external, and adjust rather than reasoning from first principles. Reference-class estimates beat inside-view estimates consistently, because imagining the steps systematically omits the ones that go wrong.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
What's the most common way this kind of project fails?

Usually an unexamined dependency or a scope that grew without the timeline moving. Ask what has to be true for the plan to hold and what happens to each item if it isn't. Failure modes are more predictable than success paths.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How far ahead is it worth forecasting?

To the point where your assumptions stop holding, which for most businesses is a few quarters. Beyond that you're producing a document rather than a forecast. Extend the horizon with scenarios instead of point estimates.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our pilot succeeded. Will it scale?

Ask what the pilot got that a full rollout won't — attention, self-selected participants, unusual support. Pilots frequently succeed on conditions that don't survive scale, and the honest test is whether the mechanism of success is reproducible.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
A supplier has raised prices 15% and we can't easily switch.

Establish what switching would actually cost before negotiating, because that number is your position and you're currently guessing at it. If it's high, the negotiation is about term and service rather than price; if it's lower than you assumed, you have more room than you think.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I decide what to charge for something new?

Anchor on the value delivered rather than your cost, then check against what the alternative costs the buyer — including doing nothing. Cost-plus pricing systematically underprices things that save people a lot and overprices things they don't need.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We have budget for one hire: engineering or sales?

Ask what's currently the constraint. If you can sell more than you can build, hire engineering; if you can build more than you can sell, hire sales. Adding to the non-constraint produces very little, and teams usually know which side is backed up.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How should we split effort between new features and technical debt?

Set a standing fraction rather than deciding case by case, because case-by-case reliably favours features — their value is concrete and debt's cost is abstract until it isn't. A fixed allocation removes the argument from every individual decision.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're considering a bonus scheme tied to individual output.

Predict what it does to collaboration. Individual incentives reliably reduce the unrewarded work that teams depend on — helping, reviewing, mentoring — and that cost lands a quarter or two later. If you do it, measure the things you're worried about before and after.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Cutting this feature would save significant maintenance.

Check who uses it and how deeply. Low usage counts sometimes hide high dependency in a few important accounts, and the maintenance saving is smaller than the relationship cost. Usage data alone underdetermines this.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Automating this would remove a job someone currently does.

Include the transition in the evaluation — retraining, morale, the knowledge that person holds that isn't written down. The arithmetic on the task alone almost always favours automation, and it's frequently the wrong arithmetic.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I stop overthinking small decisions?

Match the effort to the stakes explicitly. For decisions below a threshold, pick quickly and move — the expected cost of a suboptimal choice is smaller than the deliberation. Reserve real analysis for the small number of decisions that justify it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I avoid anchoring on the first option I see?

Generate the alternatives before evaluating any of them. Once you've assessed the first, every subsequent option gets compared to it rather than to the criteria. Writing down what a good answer requires, before looking, is the practical defence.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our decisions take weeks because everyone needs to weigh in.

Separate who decides from who's consulted. Broad consultation with a single named decider is fast; consensus requirements are slow and produce compromises nobody chose. Most decisions do not need agreement, only input.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We chose an option and now new information suggests it was wrong.

Reassess on current information without treating the reversal as an admission of error — the original decision may have been correct on what was known. The relevant question is whether switching now beats continuing, which is arithmetic rather than a verdict on the past.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Everyone prefers option A but the analysis favours B.

Find out what the preference is tracking. Consistent intuition against an analysis often means the model is missing a real cost — implementation difficulty, morale, something operational. If nobody can name it after being asked directly, then follow the analysis.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it worth doing a formal cost-benefit analysis for this?

Do it when the decision is large, contested, or will be revisited — the value is in making assumptions explicit rather than in the final number. For small uncontested decisions the analysis costs more than the improvement it produces.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're deciding between improving what works and fixing what doesn't.

Compare the marginal returns. Strengthening something already good often returns less than repairing something failing, but not always — a failing thing may be failing because there's no demand, in which case fixing it buys nothing.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should I take a smaller certain outcome now or negotiate for more?

Estimate what negotiating costs if it goes badly — not just the gap, but the relationship and the delay. Where the downside is limited, negotiating has positive expected value almost always. Where a refusal ends the opportunity, the calculation changes sharply.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do we decide what to measure?

Pick things that would change a decision if they moved. Metrics that wouldn't alter any action are reporting overhead, and they crowd out the ones that matter. Start from the decisions you make repeatedly and work backward.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should I take on a client who pays well but takes up all my capacity?

Work out what you can't do while they occupy it. A high rate on all your capacity is worse than a slightly lower rate that leaves room for the work that compounds — referrals, higher-value clients, capability building. Concentration also means their departure is your whole revenue.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
When should we rewrite rather than keep patching?

When the cost of change is rising faster than the value you're adding, and you can quantify that — velocity trend, defect rate, time to onboard. Rewrites usually take longer than estimated and lose undocumented behaviour, so the case needs to be strong rather than aesthetic.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We can launch in a month with 70% of the features or in four months with everything.

Ask what the missing 30% is worth in the first three months. If early users don't need it, the four-month version costs three months of learning and revenue to deliver value nobody was waiting for. If the product is incoherent without it, shipping early buys you negative information.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it better to have three people on one project or one person on three?

Depends on whether the work parallelizes and how much coordination it needs. Three on one finishes sooner if the work divides cleanly, and slower if they spend the gain on coordination. One on three finishes nothing for a long time and pays switching costs throughout.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our test suite takes an hour. Is it worth investing in speed?

Multiply an hour by how often it runs and by how many people wait on it, then compare against the engineering cost of halving it. Slow suites also have a second-order cost that's larger than the arithmetic — people run them less, so defects escape further.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I switched approaches three times on this project and made no progress.

Frequent switching has its own cost — each restart discards accumulated context and you never reach the part where an approach pays off. Pick the most defensible one and commit to a fixed period with a pre-set criterion for abandoning it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I compare a job offer with better pay against one with better learning?

Convert learning into money over a horizon. Ask what the skills are worth in salary terms in three years, and whether the higher-paying role also builds them. The comparison is usually less lopsided than it feels once the learning is priced rather than treated as a soft factor.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our projections have been wrong three quarters running.

Check whether they're wrong in a consistent direction. Consistent bias is correctable with a multiplier drawn from your own history; random error means the underlying process is genuinely unpredictable and the response is wider ranges rather than better point estimates.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're spread across five initiatives and none are progressing.

Sequence them. Five parallel initiatives with insufficient capacity each take five times as long and deliver value only at the end, so nothing lands. Two finished initiatives are worth more than five at 40%, and the finished ones start returning immediately.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
If we lower our response time target, what breaks?

Probably staffing during the tail hours and the quality of responses under pressure. Aggressive targets get met by degrading something unmeasured, so decide in advance what you're willing to trade and measure that too.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I want a framework for making better trade-offs.

Write down the criteria and their weights before you look at the options. Most bad trade-offs come from criteria invented after the fact to justify a preference, and the ordering is what prevents it. The weights matter less than fixing them in advance.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
A stakeholder wants a guarantee I can't give.

Offer a range with the assumptions attached, and be specific about what would move it. A confident point estimate you don't believe is worse than an honest range, because it will be treated as a commitment and you'll be measured against it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it worth paying for the enterprise tier for one feature?

Compute what the feature saves annually and compare it to the price difference, then check whether a cheaper workaround gets most of the benefit. Enterprise tiers bundle a lot you won't use, so the honest comparison is that one feature against the delta, not against the whole plan's value.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our conversion rate is 2% and we want to double revenue.

You can double conversion or double traffic, and they cost very differently. Conversion work compounds against all future traffic and usually has more headroom at 2%; traffic acquisition is more predictable but you rent it. Check which constraint is actually binding before spending.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we fix the bug affecting 3% of users or ship the feature 40% asked for?

Depends on severity, not just reach. A defect that loses data or blocks a core path for 3% outranks a convenience feature for 40%, because the cost per affected user is orders of magnitude apart. Reach alone is a poor ranking function.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're deciding between annual and monthly billing.

Annual improves cash position and reduces churn, and costs you a discount plus a higher barrier at signup. If your product's value is obvious within a month, monthly converts better and you can upgrade people later. If value takes longer to appear, annual is buying the time to demonstrate it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our best engineer wants to move to a different team internally.

Compare the cost of losing them from your team against the cost of losing them from the company, which is the actual alternative if you block it. Internal moves you resist usually become external moves within a year, and you lose the option to plan the transition.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We can reduce support load by making the product simpler or by improving docs.

Simplification reduces the ticket at source and costs product surface; docs reduce the cost per ticket and leave the confusion in place. Look at whether tickets cluster on a few flows — if they do, simplification has the better return; if they're diffuse, docs do.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it better to raise prices or reduce churn?

Run both numbers against your base. A price rise applies immediately and risks churn; a churn reduction compounds and takes longer to land. If your pricing is clearly below the value delivered, take the rise first, since it's the faster and more certain of the two.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We have technical debt in a system we might replace next year.

Then most of the debt isn't worth paying down — you'd be improving something you plan to discard. Fix only what's costing you now or what would block the replacement. The exception is anything that makes the migration harder, which pays for itself twice.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How much should we invest in reducing onboarding time?

Multiply the time saved by how many people onboard per year, and add the effect on drop-off, which is usually the larger term. If a meaningful share of signups abandon during setup, onboarding work is acquisition spend with a much better return than advertising.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're choosing between two roadmaps: incremental improvement or a big bet.

Ask what the incremental path's ceiling is. If it converges on something that still loses to the market, its predictability is a slow failure and the bet is the rational choice. If it reaches a good position, the bet has to beat that, not beat zero.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our infrastructure costs are rising faster than revenue.

Find out whether it's usage growth or inefficiency, because they have opposite implications. Usage-driven growth that outpaces revenue means the pricing model is misaligned with cost, which is a pricing problem. Inefficiency is an engineering problem with a straightforward return.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should I finish this degree or take the job offer?

Value the degree at what it adds to earnings and optionality beyond what the job provides, then subtract the salary forgone plus the tuition. For many fields that arithmetic favours the job; for licensed or credential-gated ones it doesn't. Check whether the degree can be completed later part-time.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
A competitor just cut prices 30%.

Don't match reflexively. Work out whether your customers are choosing on price or on something else, and what matching does to your margin and your ability to fund the thing that differentiates you. Price wars are won by whoever has the lower cost base, so check whether that's you before entering one.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I decide whether to open source part of our stack?

Weigh the adoption and hiring benefit against the maintenance obligation, which is the part that gets underestimated — public projects generate issues, review load, and compatibility constraints indefinitely. Open sourcing something you'd otherwise abandon is usually worse than archiving it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We have a choice between fixing the root cause or a workaround that ships tomorrow.

Ship the workaround if the bleeding is real, and schedule the root cause with a date attached. The failure mode isn't choosing the workaround, it's the scheduled fix never happening because the pressure disappeared. Write it down as debt with an owner.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our sales cycle is six months and we're running low on runway.

Then the cycle length is the binding constraint, not the conversion rate. Look for a smaller offering that closes in weeks to bridge cash, even at worse unit economics. Optimizing the six-month pipeline doesn't help if you don't reach the end of it.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're considering a rebrand.

Rebrands are expensive, disruptive, and rarely move the metric people hope for. Ask what specific problem it solves and whether a cheaper intervention addresses it. If the name genuinely blocks a market you're entering, it's justified; if it's dissatisfaction with the look, it usually isn't.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we accept a lower-margin contract to keep the team busy?

Compare it against the cost of idle capacity, which is real but not the same as the full salary — you keep the team and their knowledge either way. Low-margin work is worth taking when the alternative is genuinely nothing, and harmful when it displaces better work or resets a client's price expectation.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our largest customer is 40% of revenue.

That concentration is the dominant risk in your business and it's probably not priced into any of your planning. Their departure isn't a bad quarter, it's an existential event. Use the revenue to diversify rather than to grow into the dependency.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I decide how much runway to keep?

Enough to reach the next milestone that changes your fundraising position, plus the overrun you should expect based on your own history. Raising from a position of six weeks of cash costs far more in dilution than the money you saved by not raising earlier.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we localize into a new market?

Cost it fully: translation, support in that timezone, payment methods, legal, and ongoing maintenance of everything you ship thereafter. Localization is a permanent tax on the roadmap, not a one-time project, which is what makes it a strategic decision rather than a marketing one.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our free tier is expensive to run.

Measure what it converts. A free tier is a customer acquisition cost, so compare its cost per converted user against your other channels. If it converts poorly it's charity with a marketing story attached; if it converts well it's often your cheapest channel.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
I can automate a task that takes me an hour a week.

An hour weekly is about fifty hours a year, so automation is worth up to roughly that much of your time, discounted for maintenance and the chance the task changes. Most such automations are worth a day or two of effort and not much more.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're deciding between depth in one market and breadth across three.

Depth compounds — reputation, referrals, domain knowledge, and product fit all reinforce each other within a segment. Breadth spreads fixed costs across markets that each get an inferior product. Unless the markets share almost everything, depth usually wins until you dominate the first.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We could ship to a small beta or go straight to general availability.

The beta buys information at the cost of delay, and its value depends on how confident you are. If you're uncertain about the core use, the beta is cheap insurance against a public failure. If you've validated it, the beta mostly delays revenue and learning at scale.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our team wants better tooling but it's a quarter of work.

Quantify what the current tooling costs — build times, manual steps, failed deploys, time to onboard — multiplied by the number of people paying it. That number is often much larger than expected and settles the question. If it isn't large, the request is preference rather than economics.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we take investment or grow slowly from revenue?

Depends on whether the market rewards speed. Where there's a land-grab dynamic, capital buys a position you can't reach otherwise. Where it doesn't, investment buys growth you'd have achieved anyway in exchange for permanent dilution and a return expectation that constrains later choices.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
A supplier offers 15% off for paying twelve months upfront.

That's roughly a 30% annualized return on the cash if you'd otherwise hold it, which is high — but it converts flexible cash into a commitment to a supplier you may want to leave. Take it if the relationship is stable and cash isn't tight; decline if either is uncertain.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How much is it worth paying to reduce a delivery risk?

Up to the probability of the failure multiplied by its cost. Estimate both explicitly, even roughly, because insurance and contingency spending is usually set by anxiety rather than arithmetic and lands far from the right number in both directions.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We're choosing between two candidates and one has domain experience.

Value the domain experience at how long it would take the other to acquire it, and weigh that against the difference in everything else. Domain knowledge is usually the fastest gap to close and the most heavily overweighted in hiring, particularly against general capability.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we prioritize the enterprise deal or ten small customers worth the same?

Ten small customers give you diversification and broader signal; the enterprise deal gives you concentration, longer cycles, and demands that shape your roadmap. At equal revenue the small customers are usually worth more strategically, unless the enterprise logo unlocks a market.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Our marketing spend has a 3-month payback.

That's good if the customers stay well beyond three months, which is the question the payback figure doesn't answer. Check retention past the payback point — a short payback on customers who churn at month four is break-even work that looks like growth.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Is it worth building an internal tool other teams could use?

Multiply the benefit by the number of teams that would adopt it, then discount heavily for the fact that most don't. Internal platforms fail on adoption rather than on quality, so validate that two other teams actually want it before building for ten.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
How do I evaluate whether a partnership is worth it?

Estimate the revenue it plausibly delivers in year one, then subtract the integration, support, and account-management cost you'll carry regardless of whether it works. Most partnerships underperform their projections substantially, so run the numbers on a fraction of the forecast and see whether it still clears.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We have budget to either raise salaries or add headcount.

Ask which constraint is binding. If you're losing people, retention spending protects capability you already have and is usually cheaper than replacing it. If you're stable but under-capacity, headcount adds output. Doing the second while losing people to the first is the common expensive error.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
Should we sign a two-year contract for a discount?

Weigh the saving against the chance you'd want to leave. If the vendor's category is changing quickly, two years is a long commitment and the discount is compensating you for real optionality. In a stable category with a mature product, it's mostly free money.
The assistant evaluates trade-offs, rewards, and long-term outcomes.
We could spend on a security audit or on features customers are asking for.

Depends on your exposure and what you've committed to. If you hold sensitive data or sell to customers who will eventually ask for the audit, it's a cost of doing business you'll pay later at a worse time. If neither applies yet, features win — but note when that changes.

How do I value equity in a private company?

Discount heavily for illiquidity, dilution in future rounds, and the probability of a zero outcome, which is the modal result. Then treat what's left as a lottery ticket rather than compensation. If the cash offer alone doesn't work for you, the equity shouldn't close the gap.

We're deciding how much to spend on redundancy.

Compare the annual cost against downtime cost multiplied by expected downtime hours. Then check where your actual failures have come from — redundancy usually protects against hardware while the outages come from configuration and deploys, which it doesn't help with at all.

Should we take on a project outside our expertise for good money?

Price in the learning time, the elevated chance of a poor outcome, and the reputational cost if it goes badly. Work outside your competence needs a substantial premium to be worth it, and the quoted rate is usually set as though it's ordinary work.

We can improve the product or improve the sales process.

Look at where deals are lost. If prospects are reaching a demo and declining, the product or its fit is the constraint. If they're not reaching a demo at all, it's the sales process, and product improvements won't be seen by anyone.

How do I decide whether to take a counteroffer?

Ask what changed other than the number. If the reasons you were leaving are unaddressed, the counteroffer buys time and leaves you having disclosed that you were looking. If the offer genuinely fixes the problem — scope, manager, trajectory — it's a real option.

Our biggest cost is people and we've been asked to cut 15%.

Model what the remaining team can actually deliver, not what you hope. Cuts that leave commitments unchanged produce attrition among the people you kept, which compounds the reduction. Take the delivery consequences to whoever set the target before choosing who goes.
